chapter_text:
CHAPTER 2 — MEDIEVAL WORLD

Introduction

The MEDIEVAL period runs roughly from the 5th to the 15th century CE — between the fall of the Western Roman Empire and the beginning of the early-modern period with the European 'discoveries' and the Renaissance. It is often divided into early (~500-1000 CE), high (~1000-1300 CE) and late (~1300-1500 CE) medieval phases.

This was a time of immense change across the world. In Europe FEUDALISM emerged from the rubble of the Roman Empire. The CHURCH became enormously powerful. ISLAM was born in the 7th century and spread across half the known world within a hundred years. CHRISTIAN and ISLAMIC civilisations competed and traded — and made war on each other through the Crusades. In India, after the Gupta age came the rise of regional kingdoms, the Delhi Sultanate (1206-1526) and ultimately the Mughal Empire (1526-1857). China saw the Tang and Song dynasties, with their advances in technology, art and commerce. Mongol horsemen built the largest contiguous land empire in history. And, towards the end of this period, the RENAISSANCE began to remake European thought.

2.1 RISE OF ISLAM

Islam was founded by the Prophet MUHAMMAD (c. 570-632 CE) in Arabia. His teachings were written down as the QURAN. After his death his followers (the CALIPHS) led an astonishing expansion: within a century Islamic armies had conquered the Sassanid Persian Empire and much of the Byzantine empire — from Spain through North Africa and the Middle East to Central Asia. Three great Islamic dynasties — Umayyad, Abbasid, Fatimid — ruled successive eras. The ABBASID CALIPHATE (750-1258), capital at Baghdad, presided over an Islamic 'Golden Age' of science, philosophy, mathematics, medicine and translation work that preserved and built on the heritage of Greek, Persian and Indian civilisation.

2.2 FEUDAL EUROPE

After the fall of Rome (476 CE), Europe fragmented into small kingdoms and lordships. Under FEUDALISM:
 - A KING granted land (fiefs) to powerful NOBLES;
 - Nobles in turn granted land to lesser VASSALS in return for military service;
 - At the base, PEASANTS / SERFS worked the land and owed labour and dues to their lord.
Feudalism was a hierarchical system held together by oaths of loyalty and reciprocal obligation. It provided a degree of order in a violent age, but also rigidly limited social mobility. The CATHOLIC CHURCH, with the Pope at its head, was the central spiritual and intellectual institution — and a major political force, owning vast lands and crowning kings.

2.3 THE CRUSADES (1096-1291)

A series of religious wars launched by Christian Europe (initially called by Pope Urban II) to recapture the Holy Land (Jerusalem and Palestine) from Muslim rule. The Crusades — perhaps eight to nine major expeditions over 200 years — failed in their stated objective but profoundly affected both Christian Europe and the Islamic world. They opened trade routes, spread knowledge (Arabic science, mathematics, medicine flowed into Europe), and weakened both sides militarily and financially. They also left a legacy of religious bitterness.

2.4 THE BYZANTINE EMPIRE

The Eastern Roman Empire — known to historians as the BYZANTINE EMPIRE — survived for a thousand years after the western fall, with its capital at CONSTANTINOPLE (modern Istanbul). It preserved Roman law, Greek learning and Orthodox Christianity. Its greatest emperor, JUSTINIAN (527-565), codified Roman law (the Corpus Juris Civilis) and rebuilt the magnificent Hagia Sophia. The Byzantines transmitted classical knowledge to medieval Europe and to the Islamic world. Constantinople finally fell to the Ottoman Turks in 1453 CE — an event often taken as the end of the Middle Ages.

2.5 MONGOL CONQUESTS

In the early 13th century, GENGHIS KHAN (r. 1206-1227) united the Mongol tribes of the Central Asian steppe. Under him and his successors, Mongol armies built the largest contiguous LAND EMPIRE in history — from Korea to Hungary. The Mongols devastated cities (Baghdad, 1258), but also brought relative peace ('Pax Mongolica') to the trade routes of Asia, enabling figures like Marco Polo to travel from Italy to China. The Mongol legacy in India would come through their descendants — the MUGHALS.

2.6 MEDIEVAL INDIA — THE DELHI SULTANATE

The defeat of Prithviraj Chauhan at the Second Battle of Tarain (1192 CE) by Muhammad of Ghor opened north India to Turkic rule. In 1206, Qutb-ud-din Aibak founded the DELHI SULTANATE — the first major Islamic state in India. Five successive dynasties ruled from Delhi:
 - SLAVE / MAMLUK dynasty (1206-1290) — Aibak, Iltutmish, Razia Sultan, Balban.
 - KHALJI dynasty (1290-1320) — Alauddin Khalji extended the sultanate to the south.
 - TUGHLAQ dynasty (1320-1413) — Muhammad bin Tughlaq's ambitious experiments; Firoz Shah's public works.
 - SAYYID dynasty (1414-1451) — a weak period.
 - LODHI dynasty (1451-1526) — the last Sultanate dynasty; Ibrahim Lodhi defeated by Babur at Panipat in 1526.

The Sultanate built the QUTUB MINAR and laid the foundations of Indo-Islamic architecture. The Sufi saints (Khwaja Muinuddin Chishti, Nizamuddin Auliya) spread Islamic spirituality through devotion and music. The BHAKTI MOVEMENT in Hinduism — Kabir, Tulsidas, Mirabai, Guru Nanak — flourished in this period as a parallel devotional response.

2.7 VIJAYANAGARA, BAHMANI AND OTHER REGIONAL POWERS

While the Delhi Sultanate ruled the north, regional kingdoms flourished elsewhere:
 - The VIJAYANAGARA EMPIRE (1336-1646) in south India — capital at Hampi — preserved Hindu culture and was a major power in the Deccan.
 - The BAHMANI SULTANATE (1347-1527) — a Muslim kingdom in the Deccan that broke into smaller states (the Deccan Sultanates).
 - The KINGDOM OF MEWAR, MARWAR and other Rajput kingdoms maintained independence in north-western India.
 - In Bengal, GAUR and PANDUA were medieval capitals.

2.8 THE MUGHAL EMPIRE (1526-1857)

BABUR, a descendant of both Timur and Genghis Khan, defeated Ibrahim Lodhi at the First Battle of PANIPAT (1526) and founded the Mughal Empire. Six great emperors built one of the largest and most prosperous empires of the early modern world:
 - BABUR (1526-1530) — founder; his memoir, the Baburnama.
 - HUMAYUN (1530-1556) — driven into exile by Sher Shah Suri, restored later.
 - AKBAR (1556-1605) — the greatest emperor; introduced religious tolerance (Din-i-Ilahi), efficient administration (mansabdari system, land revenue under Todar Mal), and integrated Rajput nobility into Mughal service.
 - JAHANGIR (1605-1627) — patron of painting.
 - SHAH JAHAN (1628-1658) — built the Taj Mahal, Red Fort, Jama Masjid.
 - AURANGZEB (1658-1707) — extended the empire to its largest extent; reversed religious tolerance; constant warfare in the Deccan drained the treasury.

After Aurangzeb's death the empire declined rapidly. By the time the British formally ended Mughal rule in 1857, the emperor's authority extended barely beyond the walls of the Red Fort.

2.9 THE RENAISSANCE AND THE END OF THE MEDIEVAL PERIOD

From the 14th century in Italy a great revival of art, science and classical learning began — the RENAISSANCE ('rebirth'). Driven by the recovery of Greek and Roman texts (often through Arab intermediaries), the rise of wealthy trading cities (Florence, Venice), and the invention of the PRINTING PRESS (Gutenberg, c. 1455), the Renaissance produced figures like Leonardo da Vinci, Michelangelo and Galileo, and laid the foundation for the Scientific Revolution and the modern world. The 'medieval' period is conventionally said to end somewhere between 1453 (fall of Constantinople), 1492 (Columbus's voyage) and 1517 (Luther's Reformation).

SUMMARY

- The medieval period (~500-1500 CE) saw the rise of feudalism in Europe, the spread of Islam, the Byzantine Empire's survival, and the Mongol conquests.
- In India, the Delhi Sultanate (1206-1526) and the Mughal Empire (1526-1857) ruled most of the subcontinent.
- The Crusades (1096-1291) brought Christian and Islamic civilisations into conflict and contact.
- The Vijayanagara empire and the Bhakti movement carried Hindu culture forward.
- The Renaissance, beginning in Italy in the 14th century, marked the transition from medieval to modern.

chapter_summary.title: Medieval World — Chapter Summary
chapter_summary.intro: This is the NIOS Class 10 Social Science (213) summary for Lesson 2. The medieval world (~500-1500 CE) saw the rise of Islam, the development of feudal society and the medieval Church in Europe, the Crusades, the survival of the Byzantine Empire, the Mongol conquests, the Delhi Sultanate and the Mughal Empire in India, and finally the Renaissance that began the transition to the modern world.

sections.heading: Rise of Islam
bullets: Islam was founded by Prophet Muhammad in Arabia in the early 7th century CE; his teachings were collected as the Quran.
Within a century of Muhammad's death (632 CE), Islamic armies had conquered an area from Spain through North Africa and the Middle East to Central Asia.
The Abbasid Caliphate (750-1258), based at Baghdad, presided over an Islamic Golden Age — translation of Greek, Persian and Indian works, advances in mathematics, astronomy, medicine and philosophy.
Algebra (from al-Khwarizmi), Arabic numerals (preserved from India), and many surgical techniques travelled to medieval Europe through Islamic scholars.

sections.heading: Feudal Europe and the Crusades
bullets: After the fall of Rome (476 CE), Europe became a patchwork of small kingdoms under feudalism — a hierarchy of king, nobles, vassals and serfs bound by oaths of loyalty.
The Catholic Church, headed by the Pope, was the central spiritual and intellectual institution of medieval Europe.

The Crusades (1096-1291) were religious wars by Christian Europe to recover the Holy Land from Muslim rule. Though militarily inconclusive, they brought lasting trade contacts and intellectual exchange.

The Byzantine Empire (Eastern Roman Empire) survived in Constantinople for 1000 years after the western fall; its emperor Justinian codified Roman law; it transmitted classical learning to Europe and Islam.

sections.heading: Mongol conquests
bullets: Genghis Khan (r. 1206-1227) united the Mongol tribes and began conquests across Asia.
His successors built the largest contiguous land empire in history, from Korea to Hungary.
Mongol rule devastated cities (Baghdad 1258) but also brought 'Pax Mongolica' — relative peace on the trade routes — enabling figures like Marco Polo to travel from Europe to China.

sections.heading: Medieval India
bullets: The Delhi Sultanate (1206-1526) — five dynasties (Slave, Khalji, Tughlaq, Sayyid, Lodhi) — was the first major Islamic state in India.
Indo-Islamic architecture combined Indian and Islamic styles — Qutub Minar, Alai Darwaza, the Tughlaqabad fort.
Sufi saints (Muinuddin Chishti, Nizamuddin Auliya) and the Hindu Bhakti movement (Kabir, Tulsidas, Mirabai, Guru Nanak) flourished as parallel devotional movements.
The Vijayanagara Empire (1336-1646) in south India was a major Hindu kingdom; Hampi was its capital.
The Mughal Empire (1526-1857) was founded by Babur after his victory at Panipat; reached its peak under Akbar, Shah Jahan and Aurangzeb.

sections.heading: Renaissance and end of medieval period
bullets: From the 14th century, the Italian Renaissance ('rebirth') revived classical learning — Leonardo da Vinci, Michelangelo, Galileo.
The printing press of Gutenberg (c. 1455) revolutionised the spread of knowledge.
The medieval period conventionally ends with the fall of Constantinople (1453), Columbus's voyage (1492), or Luther's Reformation (1517) — events that mark the transition to early modernity.

key_takeaways: Islam arose in 7th-century Arabia and spread within a century from Spain to Central Asia; the Islamic Golden Age preserved and advanced classical learning.
Feudalism organised medieval European society around a hierarchy of lords and vassals.
The Byzantine Empire survived 1000 years after Rome's fall and was the eastern bridge between classical and modern learning.
The Mongol conquests built the world's largest land empire and revived the silk road.
In India the Delhi Sultanate (1206-1526) gave way to the Mughal Empire (1526-1857), the greatest of whose emperors was Akbar.
The Bhakti and Sufi movements flourished in medieval India as parallel devotional traditions.
The Renaissance, beginning in 14th-century Italy, marked the transition from the medieval to the modern world.

worksheet.title: Worksheet — Medieval World
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. Cite specific dates, dynasties or rulers where appropriate.

questions.question: Who founded Islam, when and where?
questions.answer: Islam was founded by the Prophet MUHAMMAD (c. 570-632 CE) in Arabia, specifically the cities of Mecca (where he was born and first preached) and Medina (to which he migrated in 622 CE — the year of the Hijrah, beginning of the Islamic calendar).

questions.question: What was the Islamic Golden Age, and what were its main achievements?
questions.answer: The Islamic Golden Age was the period (~750-1258 CE) under the Abbasid Caliphate (Baghdad) during which Islamic civilisation made major advances in: (1) MATHEMATICS — al-Khwarizmi formalised algebra (the word comes from Arabic al-jabr) and transmitted Indian numerals to Europe; (2) MEDICINE — Ibn Sina (Avicenna)'s Canon of Medicine became a standard textbook in European universities for 500 years; (3) ASTRONOMY — Islamic astronomers built observatories and corrected Greek star catalogues; (4) PHILOSOPHY — preservation and commentary on Aristotle (Ibn Rushd / Averroes); (5) translation movements that preserved Greek, Persian and Indian texts.

questions.question: Explain the structure of feudal society in medieval Europe.
questions.answer:
Feudal society was a strict hierarchy bound together by oaths of loyalty and reciprocal obligation:
  TOP: The KING — in theory owned all land.
  Next: NOBLES (counts, dukes, barons) — held large fiefs from the king in return for military service.
  Then: KNIGHTS and lesser VASSALS — held smaller fiefs from nobles in return for personal military service.
  Base: PEASANTS and SERFS — worked the land for their lord, owed labour and produce; serfs were tied to the land and could not leave.
The CATHOLIC CHURCH stood alongside this hierarchy — bishops and abbots held vast estates and the Pope was a major political force.

questions.question: What were the Crusades? Were they successful?
questions.answer:
The Crusades were a series of religious wars (1096-1291) launched by Christian Europe — initially called by Pope Urban II in 1095 — to recapture the Holy Land (Jerusalem and Palestine) from Muslim rule. There were perhaps eight to nine major Crusades over two centuries.

Militarily UNSUCCESSFUL: the First Crusade did capture Jerusalem (1099), but Muslim leaders (notably Saladin in 1187) recovered it, and by 1291 the last Christian crusader stronghold (Acre) had fallen. Christians did not retain the Holy Land.

BROADER CONSEQUENCES: (1) Long-distance trade between Europe and the Levant grew; (2) Islamic learning (Arabic mathematics, medicine, philosophy) flowed into Europe; (3) Italian city-states (Venice, Genoa) grew rich on the trade; (4) the moral authority of the Papacy was eventually weakened; (5) lasting religious bitterness was created on both sides.

questions.question: Why is the Byzantine Empire historically important?
questions.answer:
The Byzantine Empire (Eastern Roman Empire, 330-1453 CE) is historically important for several reasons:
(1) SURVIVAL — it preserved Roman political institutions for 1000 years after the fall of the Western Roman Empire.
(2) JUSTINIAN'S LAW — Emperor Justinian (527-565) codified Roman law into the Corpus Juris Civilis, which became the basis of much of European civil law.
(3) PRESERVATION OF CLASSICAL LEARNING — Byzantine scholars preserved Greek manuscripts (Plato, Aristotle, Greek scientific and literary works) through the medieval period; many would not have survived otherwise.
(4) ARCHITECTURE AND ART — the Hagia Sophia is one of the masterpieces of world architecture; Byzantine mosaics and icon art influenced both Christian and Islamic traditions.
(5) ORTHODOX CHRISTIANITY — the Byzantines were the source from which Slavic peoples (Russians, Serbs, Bulgarians) received Eastern Orthodoxy.
(6) BUFFER — it acted as a long-standing buffer between Asia and Europe, slowing the westward expansion of various nomadic and Islamic powers.

questions.question: Briefly describe Genghis Khan and the Mongol conquests.
questions.answer: GENGHIS KHAN (born Temujin, c. 1162-1227) united the Mongol tribes of the Central Asian steppe through diplomacy and warfare, becoming Great Khan in 1206. Under him and his successors (his sons and grandsons including Ogedei, Mongke and Kublai), the Mongols built the largest CONTIGUOUS LAND EMPIRE in history — at its peak stretching from Korea in the east to Hungary in the west, including China, Persia, Russia and Central Asia. Mongol conquest was often extremely violent — entire cities were destroyed (Baghdad sacked in 1258, ending the Abbasid Caliphate). But under Mongol rule the trade routes of Asia became safer than they had been for centuries ('Pax Mongolica'), and Marco Polo of Venice could travel safely to the court of Kublai Khan in China.

questions.question: List the five dynasties of the Delhi Sultanate in order and name one ruler from each.
questions.answer:
(1) SLAVE / MAMLUK dynasty (1206-1290) — Qutb-ud-din Aibak (founder); Iltutmish; Razia Sultan (the first female Muslim ruler of Delhi); Balban.
(2) KHALJI dynasty (1290-1320) — Jalaluddin Khalji; Alauddin Khalji (extended sultanate to the south).
(3) TUGHLAQ dynasty (1320-1413) — Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq; Muhammad bin Tughlaq (known for ambitious experiments — moving capital, token currency); Firoz Shah Tughlaq.
(4) SAYYID dynasty (1414-1451) — Khizr Khan; weak period.
(5) LODHI dynasty (1451-1526) — Bahlul Lodhi; Sikandar Lodhi; Ibrahim Lodhi (defeated by Babur at Panipat).

questions.question: What was the Bhakti movement? Name three major Bhakti saints.
questions.answer:
The Bhakti movement was a medieval Hindu devotional movement that emphasised PERSONAL LOVE OF GOD (bhakti = devotion) and rejected priestly authority, ritualism and caste discrimination. It used regional languages (Tamil, Marathi, Hindi, Bengali, Punjabi) rather than Sanskrit, making religion accessible to all. Three major Bhakti saints:
 - KABIR (15th c.) — wove doha verses critical of both Hindu and Muslim ritualism; born to a Muslim weaver family, drew inspiration from Hindu and Sufi traditions.
 - TULSIDAS (16th c.) — composed the Ramcharitmanas (the Ramayana in Awadhi).
 - MIRABAI (16th c.) — Rajput princess who composed devotional songs to Krishna.
Others: Guru Nanak (founder of Sikhism), Surdas, Chaitanya, Ravidas, Andal.

questions.question: Why is Akbar considered the greatest of the Mughal emperors?
questions.answer:
Akbar (1556-1605) is considered the greatest Mughal emperor for several reasons:
(1) MILITARY EXPANSION — he extended the empire across north and central India.
(2) RELIGIOUS TOLERANCE — abolished the jizya (tax on non-Muslims); promoted Hindu-Muslim harmony; gave high office to Rajput and Hindu nobles; experimented with the syncretic Din-i-Ilahi.
(3) ADMINISTRATION — introduced the MANSABDARI system of military-administrative ranks; entrusted Raja Todar Mal with land-revenue reform (zabt system) — a systematic, more equitable land tax.
(4) INTEGRATED THE RAJPUTS — married Rajput princesses; allied with Rajput kings rather than crushing them.
(5) CULTURAL PATRONAGE — sponsored a flowering of Mughal painting; built Fatehpur Sikri.
These policies created the political, administrative and cultural foundations on which the empire stood for 150 years.

questions.question: What was the Renaissance, and how did it mark the end of the medieval period?
questions.answer:
The RENAISSANCE ('rebirth') was a movement of cultural and intellectual revival that began in Italian city-states (Florence, Venice, Rome) in the 14th century and spread across Europe over the next 300 years. Its key features:

(1) REVIVAL OF CLASSICAL LEARNING — Greek and Roman texts (preserved by Byzantine and Arab scholars) were translated, studied and built upon.

(2) HUMANISM — a renewed focus on human achievement, individual creativity, and the dignity of human reason — as opposed to a purely religious worldview.

(3) ART AND ARCHITECTURE — Leonardo da Vinci, Michelangelo, Raphael, Donatello produced works of unprecedented mastery; Brunelleschi pioneered Renaissance architecture.

(4) SCIENCE — Copernicus proposed the heliocentric model; Galileo demonstrated it; Vesalius reformed anatomy. The Scientific Revolution grew directly out of Renaissance attitudes.

(5) PRINTING — Johannes Gutenberg's printing press (c. 1455) revolutionised the spread of ideas. Within decades, millions of books were in circulation.

(6) EXPLORATION — Renaissance-era confidence and improved navigation enabled European voyages — Columbus (1492), Vasco da Gama (1498), Magellan (1519-22) — that connected the world's continents.

HOW IT MARKED THE END OF THE MEDIEVAL PERIOD: it shifted European thought from a primarily religious / Church-centred worldview to one that valued reason, observation, classical antiquity, individual achievement, and the natural world. The fall of CONSTANTINOPLE (1453), the discovery of the Americas (1492) and Luther's Reformation (1517) are conventional markers of where medieval ends and modern begins — and the Renaissance is the intellectual undercurrent that made the transition possible.

questions.question: The founder of Islam was the Prophet ____.
The capital of the Abbasid Caliphate was ____.
Algebra was formalised by the Islamic mathematician ____.
Land granted in return for military service in feudal Europe was called a ____.
The head of the medieval Catholic Church was the ____.
The Byzantine Empire was the Eastern half of the ____ Empire.
questions.explanation: Survived 1000 years after the western fall.

questions.question: The Byzantine emperor who codified Roman law was ____.
The founder of the Mongol Empire was ____.
The Delhi Sultanate was founded in the year ____.
The Khalji ruler who extended the Sultanate to the south was Alauddin ____.
Guru ____ was the founder of Sikhism.
The Mughal Empire was founded by ____ after his victory at the First Battle of Panipat.
The Taj Mahal was built by ____ in memory of Mumtaz Mahal.
The Renaissance began in ____ in the 14th century.
The printing press was invented by ____ around 1455.
How quickly did Islam spread after Muhammad's death?
questions.answer: Astonishingly quickly. Within ONE CENTURY of Muhammad's death (632 CE), Islamic armies had conquered an area stretching from SPAIN in the west, across NORTH AFRICA, through the MIDDLE EAST, and into CENTRAL ASIA in the east — an empire larger than the Roman Empire at its peak. They defeated the Sassanid Persian Empire entirely and conquered most of the Byzantine empire's eastern provinces.

questions.question: What contributions of the Islamic Golden Age reached medieval Europe?
questions.answer: Many. (1) ARITHMETIC: Indian-origin decimal numerals (so-called 'Arabic numerals'). (2) ALGEBRA: al-Khwarizmi's treatises. (3) MEDICINE: Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine, Razi's clinical writings. (4) ASTRONOMY: corrected star catalogues, astronomical instruments. (5) PHILOSOPHY: preservation and commentary on Aristotle (Ibn Rushd / Averroes; Ibn Sina / Avicenna). (6) SCIENCE: optics (Ibn al-Haytham). Much of this knowledge entered Europe through Spain (translated into Latin in 12th-13th century Toledo) and via the Crusades.

questions.question: What was the role of the Catholic Church in medieval Europe?
questions.answer: The Catholic Church was the central institution of medieval European life. (1) SPIRITUAL — controlled access to sacraments, taught about salvation, dictated moral life. (2) INTELLECTUAL — monasteries copied manuscripts; cathedral schools (later universities) trained scholars; theology was the queen of sciences. (3) POLITICAL — the Pope crowned kings and emperors; the Church owned vast lands; bishops were political lords. (4) SOCIAL — ran hospitals, schools, orphanages and famine relief; saints' shrines structured local life.

questions.question: What were the long-term consequences of the Crusades despite their military failure?
questions.answer:
Although the Crusades failed in their stated military objective, they had lasting consequences:
(1) TRADE — Italian city-states (Venice, Genoa, Pisa) grew rich shipping Crusaders, supplies and commerce across the Mediterranean. They became dominant trading powers.
(2) INTELLECTUAL EXCHANGE — Western Europe was introduced to advanced Islamic science, mathematics, medicine and philosophy, accelerating the eventual Renaissance.
(3) DECLINE OF FEUDALISM — many nobles sold land or died on Crusade, weakening the feudal system.
(4) PAPAL AUTHORITY — initially boosted, then declined in the later Crusades as cynicism grew.
(5) PERMANENT RELIGIOUS BITTERNESS between Western Christendom and the Islamic world (and also with Eastern Orthodox Christianity — the Fourth Crusade sacked Constantinople in 1204).
(6) Inspired the LATER AGE OF EXPLORATION as Europe sought direct trade routes to bypass the Muslim middlemen.

questions.question: What was the 'Pax Mongolica' and why was it important?
questions.answer: 'Pax Mongolica' (Mongol Peace) refers to the 13th-14th century period during which the Mongol Empire — controlling the trade routes from China to the Black Sea — enforced sufficient order that long-distance travel across the Eurasian land mass was safer than it had been for centuries. It was important because: (1) European traders could reach China (Marco Polo's journey in the 1270s); (2) Goods, technologies (paper, printing, gunpowder, the compass) and ideas flowed westward; (3) Diseases too — the Black Death (1346-53) probably reached Europe along Mongol trade routes.

questions.question: Name the five dynasties of the Delhi Sultanate in chronological order.
questions.answer: (1) Slave / Mamluk dynasty (1206-1290) — founded by Qutb-ud-din Aibak. (2) Khalji dynasty (1290-1320) — Alauddin Khalji. (3) Tughlaq dynasty (1320-1413) — Muhammad bin Tughlaq, Firoz Shah Tughlaq. (4) Sayyid dynasty (1414-1451). (5) Lodhi dynasty (1451-1526) — ended when Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodhi at Panipat.

questions.question: What is Indo-Islamic architecture? Name three examples.
questions.answer: Indo-Islamic architecture is a hybrid style that emerged from the 12th century onwards, combining INDIAN traditions of construction and craftsmanship (corbelled arches, intricate stone carving, lotus and floral motifs) with ISLAMIC features (true arches, domes, minarets, geometric and calligraphic ornament). Builders mostly Indian craftsmen, patrons mostly Muslim rulers — a genuine fusion. THREE EXAMPLES: (1) The QUTUB MINAR and the Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque (Aibak / Iltutmish, 13th c.); (2) the TOMB OF SHER SHAH SURI at Sasaram; (3) HUMAYUN'S TOMB in Delhi (a Mughal antecedent of the Taj Mahal). The TAJ MAHAL itself, Akbar's Fatehpur Sikri, and the Red Fort are the culminating Mughal examples.

questions.question: Why were the Bhakti and Sufi movements significant in medieval India?
questions.answer:
(1) SOCIAL — both reached beyond the elite to common people, using regional languages (Bhakti) and popular music / poetry (Sufi qawwali). Both implicitly challenged caste hierarchy and external religious distinction.
(2) CULTURAL — generated a treasure of devotional poetry that became part of the everyday spiritual life of Indians (Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas, Mirabai's bhajans, Kabir's dohas, the Sikh Guru Granth Sahib).
(3) RELIGIOUS HARMONY — many Bhakti and Sufi saints emphasised the unity of all religions (Kabir, Guru Nanak). They softened the Hindu-Muslim divide, sometimes producing genuine syncretic communities.
(4) DEMOCRATISATION OF SPIRITUALITY — by emphasising personal devotion over priestly mediation, they made religion an accessible matter of the heart for ordinary villagers and townspeople.
Both movements continue to shape Indian religious life today.

questions.question: Name the six great Mughal emperors in chronological order.
questions.answer: (1) Babur (1526-1530); (2) Humayun (1530-1556, with an exile in between); (3) Akbar (1556-1605); (4) Jahangir (1605-1627); (5) Shah Jahan (1628-1658); (6) Aurangzeb (1658-1707). After Aurangzeb the empire declined; many lesser emperors followed, the last being Bahadur Shah Zafar (exiled 1857).

questions.question: Why did the Mughal Empire decline after Aurangzeb?
questions.answer:
Several causes:
(1) AURANGZEB'S DECCAN WARS — 27 years of campaigning in the Deccan drained the treasury and demoralised the army.
(2) REVERSAL OF RELIGIOUS TOLERANCE — Aurangzeb reimposed the jizya, destroyed some temples, and alienated Hindu allies including the Rajputs and the Marathas.
(3) MARATHA REBELLION under Shivaji and his successors created a rival power in the Deccan that the Mughals could never finally defeat.
(4) WEAK SUCCESSORS — after Aurangzeb's death (1707) a series of weak emperors saw power slip to provincial governors who became independent rulers (the Nawabs of Awadh, Bengal, the Nizam of Hyderabad).
(5) EXTERNAL INVASIONS — Nader Shah of Persia sacked Delhi (1739), looting the Peacock Throne and the Kohinoor diamond; Ahmad Shah Abdali invaded repeatedly.
(6) BRITISH EAST INDIA COMPANY — exploited the political fragmentation, defeating Bengal at Plassey (1757) and gradually replacing the Mughals as the dominant power.

questions.question: Explain the role of the printing press in the Renaissance.
questions.answer:
Johannes Gutenberg's printing press (c. 1455) used movable metal type and an oil-based ink to produce books mechanically. Before Gutenberg, books were hand-copied — slow, expensive, and rare. After Gutenberg, books could be produced in hundreds or thousands of copies at a fraction of the cost. By 1500, perhaps 8-10 MILLION printed books were in circulation in Europe.

IMPACT ON RENAISSANCE:
(1) Classical Greek and Roman texts (recovered from Byzantine and Arab sources) could now be widely studied.
(2) Vernacular literature flourished — works in Italian, English, French could reach broad audiences.
(3) SCIENTIFIC IDEAS spread rapidly — Copernicus, Galileo, Vesalius could be read across Europe.
(4) Luther's Reformation (1517) was the first major movement to fully exploit print — the 95 Theses spread across Germany in weeks.
(5) Literacy gradually expanded as books became affordable.
The printing press is often called the most important invention of the Renaissance — without it, the spread of knowledge that made the modern world would have been impossible.

questions.question: Discuss the administrative system of Akbar.
questions.answer:
Akbar (1556-1605) built one of the most efficient pre-modern bureaucracies in the world. Key features:

1. MANSABDARI SYSTEM
  - Every officer (mansabdar) was assigned a numerical rank (mansab) — for example 100, 500, 5000 — indicating both his personal status (zat) and the number of cavalry troops (sawar) he had to maintain.
  - Mansabdars were paid either in cash or via revenue assignments (jagirs) over particular territories.
  - This created a uniform, transferable officer corps loyal directly to the emperor, not to hereditary fiefs.

2. LAND REVENUE (ZABT system, under Raja Todar Mal)
  - Land was measured in standard units (bighas).
  - Average produce per bigha was calculated for different crops over ten years.
  - The state's share was set at roughly one-third of the produce, payable in cash.
  - This was systematic and predictable — better than arbitrary assessment, though it could be harsh in famine years.

3. PROVINCIAL ADMINISTRATION
  - The empire was divided into 15 SUBAS (provinces), each under a subahdar (governor).
  - Each suba had separate officers for revenue (diwan), military, justice (qazi) and religious affairs.
  - Below the suba, sarkars (districts) and parganas (sub-districts).

4. RELIGIOUS TOLERANCE
  - Abolished the jizya tax on non-Muslims (1564).
  - Removed the pilgrim tax.
  - Hindus, especially Rajputs, were given high mansabs — Raja Todar Mal (revenue), Raja Man Singh (general), Birbal (courtier).
  - Held religious discussions at his Ibadat Khana with scholars of all faiths, eventually formulating the eclectic Din-i-Ilahi.

5. INTEGRATION OF RAJPUTS
  - Married Rajput princesses (Jodha Bai of Amber).
  - Treated Rajput chiefs as honoured allies, not subjects to be crushed.
  - This created a permanent base of non-Muslim support.

Result: a stable, prosperous, multi-religious empire that lasted 150 years after Akbar's death.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

In the 8th-13th centuries Baghdad was the cultural capital of the Islamic world. Scholars translated Greek, Persian and Indian works into Arabic. Al-Khwarizmi formalised algebra, Ibn Sina wrote on medicine, and Ibn al-Haytham revolutionised optics.

(i) Which caliphate had its capital at Baghdad?
(ii) Name two contributions of Islamic scholars to mathematics.
(iii) Why did Islamic civilisation make so many scientific advances during this period?
(iv) How did this Islamic learning reach medieval Europe?
questions.answer:
(i) The ABBASID Caliphate (750-1258 CE).
(ii) (a) ALGEBRA — al-Khwarizmi systematised it; the word algebra comes from his book Kitab al-Jabr. (b) Transmission of the DECIMAL PLACE-VALUE SYSTEM and ZERO from India to Europe (so-called 'Arabic numerals'). (c) Trigonometry — Islamic mathematicians refined sine, cosine, tangent.
(iii) Because the Abbasids actively SPONSORED translation (the House of Wisdom in Baghdad), brought together scholars from across the empire (Persians, Indians, Christians, Jews, Greeks), and rewarded original work. Islamic civilisation was also a meeting-point of Greek, Persian and Indian traditions; combined with internal innovation and material prosperity, it produced what historians call the Islamic Golden Age.
(iv) Mainly through three routes: (a) SPAIN — Islamic Spain (al-Andalus) hosted scholars of all faiths; the city of Toledo became a major translation centre in the 12th-13th centuries, where Arabic works were rendered into Latin. (b) SICILY — under the Normans (and earlier Arab rule) became a similar bridge. (c) THE CRUSADES — direct contact with the Islamic east brought back books and ideas. Once in Latin, this knowledge powered Europe's high medieval renaissance (12th c.) and ultimately the Renaissance.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

In medieval Europe, kings granted fiefs (land) to nobles in return for military service; nobles in turn granted smaller fiefs to lesser vassals; at the base, peasants and serfs worked the land. Above the political hierarchy stood the Catholic Church with its Pope.

(i) What was a 'fief'?
(ii) Who was at the base of feudal society?
(iii) How did the Church fit into the feudal system?
(iv) What were the strengths and weaknesses of feudalism?
questions.answer:
(i) A FIEF was a piece of land (or sometimes a privilege or office) granted by a lord to a vassal in return for an OATH of loyalty and military service. The vassal could collect the produce of the fief; in return he had to provide armed men to fight for the lord.
(ii) PEASANTS and especially SERFS — agricultural labourers who worked the land of their lord. Serfs were legally tied to the land and could not leave without permission. They owed labour days, a share of produce and various fees to their lord.
(iii) The Church was not separate from the feudal system but woven through it. (a) Bishops and abbots held FIEFS — they were feudal lords themselves. (b) The Pope acted as a kind of supreme overlord, claiming the authority to crown and depose kings. (c) The Church owned perhaps a third of all land in many regions. (d) Spiritually, the Church gave the whole system religious sanction — kings ruled 'by divine right', and serfs were taught to accept their place.
(iv) STRENGTHS: provided order in a violent post-Roman age; created mutual obligations (lords protected, vassals served); rooted political authority in personal loyalty. WEAKNESSES: rigid hierarchy with almost no social mobility; constant private warfare among nobles; harsh on serfs; weak central state; could not adapt to large-scale commerce and an emerging money economy.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

In 1095 Pope Urban II called on Christian knights to free the Holy Land from Muslim rule. The First Crusade captured Jerusalem in 1099. Subsequent Crusades failed to retain it permanently — Saladin recaptured Jerusalem in 1187. Yet the Crusades shaped Europe's medieval centuries.

(i) Who called the First Crusade?
(ii) When was Jerusalem first captured by the Crusaders and when recaptured by Saladin?
(iii) Were the Crusades militarily successful in their stated objective?
(iv) What unintended consequences did the Crusades produce?
questions.answer:
(i) POPE URBAN II, at the Council of Clermont in 1095.
(ii) Captured by the Crusaders in 1099 (First Crusade); recaptured by SALADIN, sultan of Egypt and Syria, in 1187. Various Crusades attempted to recover it but only briefly succeeded.
(iii) NO — by 1291 the last Christian stronghold in the Holy Land (Acre) fell to the Muslims. Western Europeans never retained Jerusalem permanently.
(iv) Many: (a) Italian city-states (Venice, Genoa) grew rich on shipping and trade — became Mediterranean powers. (b) Islamic knowledge of mathematics, medicine, philosophy flowed into Europe. (c) Many nobles sold or mortgaged land to fund their journeys — weakening feudalism. (d) The Fourth Crusade (1204) sacked the Christian Byzantine capital Constantinople — a permanent rift between western Catholicism and eastern Orthodoxy. (e) The military orders (Templars, Hospitallers) became powerful banking and landowning corporations. (f) Long-lasting religious bitterness between Christianity and Islam.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

In the early 13th century, the Mongol leader Genghis Khan united the steppe tribes and unleashed conquests that within a few decades had built the largest contiguous land empire in history. Mongol cavalry could cover vast distances and used new tactics.

(i) When did Genghis Khan become 'Great Khan'?
(ii) Why were Mongol armies so successful in conquest?
(iii) Name two major cities destroyed by the Mongols.
(iv) What was the Pax Mongolica and what did it make possible?
questions.answer:
(i) 1206 CE — when he united the Mongol tribes and was proclaimed Great Khan at a kuriltai (tribal assembly).
(ii) Several reasons: (a) MOBILITY — every soldier had two or three remount horses and could cover huge distances at speed. (b) DISCIPLINE — strict obedience, well-coordinated tactics like feigned retreat and encirclement. (c) MERITOCRACY — Genghis promoted by ability, not birth. (d) ADAPTIVE TECHNOLOGY — they recruited engineers from conquered cities and quickly learned siege warfare. (e) PSYCHOLOGICAL WARFARE — the threat of massacre often induced surrender.
(iii) Examples: BAGHDAD (1258) — the Abbasid capital, sacked by Hulagu Khan, ending the Caliphate; SAMARKAND, BUKHARA, HERAT in Central Asia; KIEV in Russia; cities in Hungary. Estimates of population loss are in the tens of millions, especially in northern China and the Islamic world.
(iv) The PAX MONGOLICA was the relative peace and security enforced across the Mongol-ruled trade routes from China to the Mediterranean in the 13th-14th centuries. It made possible: long-distance overland trade (silk road revival); travellers like MARCO POLO of Venice reaching China; westward flow of inventions (gunpowder, paper, printing, the compass); and the eastward spread of European diplomats and missionaries. It also enabled the spread of the BLACK DEATH in the 14th century.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

The Delhi Sultanate was established in 1206 after Muhammad of Ghor's victory at the Second Battle of Tarain. Five successive dynasties ruled from Delhi over the next 320 years. The Sultanate built the Qutub Minar and shaped medieval north India.

(i) Who founded the Delhi Sultanate?
(ii) Name the five Sultanate dynasties in order.
(iii) Who was Razia Sultan?
(iv) How did the Sultanate end?
questions.answer:
(i) Qutb-ud-din AIBAK, a Turkic slave-general of Muhammad of Ghor, declared himself Sultan of Delhi in 1206 after Muhammad's death.
(ii) (1) Slave/Mamluk (1206-1290); (2) Khalji (1290-1320); (3) Tughlaq (1320-1413); (4) Sayyid (1414-1451); (5) Lodhi (1451-1526).
(iii) Razia Sultan (Razia al-Din, r. 1236-1240) was the daughter of Iltutmish and the FIRST FEMALE Muslim ruler of Delhi. Her father considered her more capable than her brothers; she was an effective ruler but was opposed by Turkish nobles unwilling to accept a woman, and was eventually overthrown.
(iv) In 1526 BABUR — a Central Asian descendant of Timur and Genghis Khan — invaded India and defeated IBRAHIM LODHI, the last Sultan of Delhi, at the First Battle of PANIPAT. Babur then founded the MUGHAL Empire.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

In medieval India two great devotional movements flourished: the BHAKTI movement among Hindus (Kabir, Tulsidas, Mirabai, Guru Nanak) and SUFISM among Muslims (Muinuddin Chishti, Nizamuddin Auliya). Both spoke to the common people in their own languages.

(i) State two common features of the Bhakti and Sufi movements.
(ii) Name three Bhakti saints and one Sufi saint.
(iii) Why did both movements appeal to common people?
(iv) What was the social impact of these movements?
questions.answer:
(i) Common features: (a) Both emphasised PERSONAL DEVOTION to God over external ritual. (b) Both used VERNACULAR languages (Hindi, Punjabi, Marathi, Tamil, Bengali) rather than only Sanskrit / Persian, so common people could understand. (c) Both were OPEN to all castes and social classes. (d) Both produced great devotional poetry and music.
(ii) Bhakti: KABIR, TULSIDAS, MIRABAI (also Guru Nanak, Surdas, Chaitanya, Ravidas, Andal). Sufi: MUINUDDIN CHISHTI (also Nizamuddin Auliya, Baba Farid).
(iii) Because they (a) spoke in the LANGUAGE OF THE PEOPLE; (b) admitted ALL castes — even untouchables and women; (c) emphasised LOVE OF GOD rather than expensive ritual or learned scripture; (d) addressed the practical SUFFERINGS and YEARNINGS of ordinary villagers and townspeople through accessible song and story.
(iv) Several major impacts: (a) PARTIAL SOFTENING of caste rigidity. (b) Promotion of HINDU-MUSLIM HARMONY — Kabir, Guru Nanak and several Sufis taught the unity of all religions. (c) Birth of new traditions — SIKHISM grew directly out of the Bhakti-Sufi confluence; many regional folk-religions absorbed both. (d) FLOURISHING of vernacular literature — the Ramcharitmanas, Mirabai's bhajans, Kabir's dohas are still loved across India. (e) Created a SHARED SPIRITUAL VOCABULARY that helped Hindus and Muslims live alongside each other.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Babur founded the Mughal Empire in 1526 after defeating Ibrahim Lodhi at the First Battle of Panipat. The empire reached its greatest extent and prosperity under Akbar (1556-1605), Shah Jahan (1628-1658) and Aurangzeb (1658-1707).

(i) Where and when was the First Battle of Panipat fought?
(ii) Who was Akbar's revenue minister and what reform did he introduce?
(iii) Name one architectural masterpiece built by Shah Jahan.
(iv) Why did the Mughal Empire decline after Aurangzeb?
questions.answer:
(i) At PANIPAT (in modern Haryana, north of Delhi), in 1526 CE. Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodhi, ending the Delhi Sultanate.
(ii) RAJA TODAR MAL. He introduced the ZABT system: land was carefully measured, average productivity of each kind of land calculated over ten years, and the state's share fixed at about one-third of the produce, payable in cash. This was systematic and predictable.
(iii) The TAJ MAHAL (built 1632-1653 in memory of his wife Mumtaz Mahal). Also the Red Fort and Jama Masjid in Delhi.
(iv) Several reasons: (a) Aurangzeb's costly DECCAN WARS lasted 27 years and drained the treasury. (b) Reversal of religious tolerance — reimposed jizya, destroyed some temples — ALIENATED HINDU ALLIES including Rajputs and Marathas. (c) Rise of the MARATHAS under Shivaji and his successors. (d) Weak SUCCESSORS after 1707 — provincial governors became independent. (e) External invasions (Nader Shah of Persia sacked Delhi in 1739; Abdali multiple times). (f) The BRITISH East India Company exploited the political fragmentation to take over India.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

From the 14th century in Italy, the Renaissance revived classical learning, art and science. Gutenberg's printing press (c. 1455) made books cheap and abundant. Columbus's voyage (1492), Luther's Reformation (1517) and the work of Galileo all flowed from this intellectual revival.

(i) Where and when did the Renaissance begin?
(ii) What did 'Renaissance' literally mean and what did it revive?
(iii) Why was the printing press so important?
(iv) Name two events that mark the end of the medieval period and the beginning of the modern.
questions.answer:
(i) In ITALY — specifically in city-states like Florence, Venice and Rome — in the 14th century (1300s).
(ii) 'Renaissance' literally means 'REBIRTH'. It revived: (a) classical Greek and Roman LEARNING (philosophy, mathematics, history, literature) preserved through Byzantine and Arab intermediaries; (b) classical IDEALS of art and beauty (Roman sculpture, balanced architecture); (c) the human-centred OUTLOOK ('humanism') of antiquity, valuing reason, individual achievement and the natural world.
(iii) Before Gutenberg, books were hand-copied — slow, expensive, rare. The printing press could produce hundreds of copies in the time it took a scribe to copy one. By 1500, perhaps 8-10 million printed books circulated in Europe. This (a) democratised LEARNING; (b) accelerated the spread of new ideas (Luther's Reformation went viral on the press); (c) preserved knowledge against the accidents of single manuscripts; (d) standardised languages and texts.
(iv) Conventional markers include: FALL OF CONSTANTINOPLE (1453); COLUMBUS's voyage (1492); LUTHER's 95 Theses (1517); also Gutenberg's printing press (c. 1455) and Copernicus's De Revolutionibus (1543). Each event represents a turning-point — political (Constantinople), geographic (Columbus), religious (Luther), technological (Gutenberg) or scientific (Copernicus).

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Akbar abolished the jizya and gave high offices to Hindus. Aurangzeb reimposed the jizya, destroyed some temples and tried to enforce a strict Sunni orthodoxy. Their contrasting policies had very different consequences for the empire.

(i) What was the jizya?
(ii) Why did Akbar abolish it?
(iii) What were the consequences of Aurangzeb reimposing it?
(iv) What general lesson does this contrast suggest about ruling a diverse society?
questions.answer:
(i) The JIZYA was a tax historically levied by Islamic states on non-Muslim subjects in return for state protection. In Mughal India it applied to Hindus (and others) but not to Muslims.
(ii) Akbar abolished it in 1564 because: (a) the empire's Hindu majority had to be integrated as loyal subjects, not treated as a separate class; (b) high Hindu officers (Todar Mal, Man Singh, Birbal) were essential to administration; (c) Akbar himself, under the influence of Sufi and Hindu thinkers, believed in religious tolerance.
(iii) Aurangzeb reimposed the jizya in 1679. Consequences: (a) ALIENATED the Hindu majority including the Rajputs, who had been Mughal allies for a century. (b) Triggered the RAJPUT war (1679-81) and pushed the Marathas into open hostility. (c) Drove Sikhs into armed resistance — Aurangzeb executed the 9th Guru, Tegh Bahadur, which radicalised Sikhism under Guru Gobind Singh. (d) Eroded the political bargain on which the empire rested; the long-term decline of Mughal power accelerated.
(iv) RELIGIOUS TOLERANCE and INTEGRATION of diverse groups into a shared political project are essential to ruling a diverse society. Forcing uniformity creates resistance and ultimately destabilises the state. Akbar's tolerance built the empire; Aurangzeb's rigidity unravelled it. The principle remains relevant to any plural, multi-religious polity — including modern India.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Leonardo da Vinci (1452-1519), Michelangelo (1475-1564), Galileo Galilei (1564-1642) and Nicolaus Copernicus (1473-1543) are some of the giants of the Renaissance and the Scientific Revolution. Each combined careful observation with reason.

(i) Match these figures to one main achievement each.
(ii) What did Copernicus propose that contradicted medieval teaching?
(iii) Why was Galileo persecuted by the Church?
(iv) How did the Renaissance lead to the Scientific Revolution?
questions.answer:
(i) Leonardo — Renaissance polymath (painter of Mona Lisa and The Last Supper; anatomical drawings; engineering designs). Michelangelo — sculptor (David, Pietà) and painter (Sistine Chapel ceiling). Galileo — confirmed by telescope that Jupiter has moons and Venus has phases, supporting the heliocentric model; pioneered experimental physics. Copernicus — published De Revolutionibus (1543), proposing that the earth and other planets orbit the sun.
(ii) Copernicus proposed the HELIOCENTRIC model: the SUN, not the earth, is at the centre of the universe; the earth and other planets orbit the sun. This contradicted the medieval and ancient Ptolemaic GEOCENTRIC view (earth at the centre, sun and planets orbiting earth) — which had been backed by Church teaching for over a thousand years.
(iii) Galileo used his telescope (1609 onwards) to find concrete EVIDENCE that the heliocentric model was correct (Jupiter's moons, the phases of Venus, sunspots, mountains on the Moon). He published these results in The Starry Messenger (1610) and later in his Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems (1632). The Catholic Inquisition, fearing the challenge to its authority and to literal readings of scripture, summoned Galileo to Rome, forced him to recant in 1633, and placed him under house arrest for the last nine years of his life.
(iv) The Renaissance revived classical learning, encouraged careful OBSERVATION of nature, valued human REASON over received authority, and (through the printing press) spread new ideas widely. These attitudes — combined with new instruments (telescope, microscope) and mathematical tools — produced the Scientific Revolution of the 16th-17th centuries, culminating in Newton's Principia Mathematica (1687). Without the Renaissance's intellectual climate, the Scientific Revolution would not have been possible.
